title: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Ethics - Biotechnology - Maintaining objective observation records
subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: While recording the mass of a chemical powder in a strictly regulated GLP (Good Laboratory Practice) lab notebook, a technician accidentally writes $14.5 \text{ g}$ instead of the correct value of $1.45 \text{ g}$ shown on the analytical balance. Which procedure is the correct, compliant method for correcting this written error?
options: Apply white-out correction fluid over the error, let it dry, and write $1.45 \text{ g}$ over it.
Scribble over the incorrect number heavily in black ink so it cannot be read, then write the correct number in the margin.
Draw a single strike-through line across $14.5 \text{ g}$, write the correct $1.45 \text{ g}$ beside it, and include the technician's initials and the current date.
Carefully trace over the '4' to make it look like a '1', and insert a new decimal point in the correct location.
questions.explain:
Under GLP and standard laboratory auditing guidelines (such as ALCOA+), all original data must remain legible, even if incorrect. 

The strict industry standard for correcting physical errors is to draw a **single horizontal line** through the mistake (so the original text is still visible), write the correct value next to it, and authenticate the change with the corrector's **initials and the date**. Sometimes a brief explanation code (e.g., "SE" for spelling error or "RE" for recording error) is also required. Using white-out, scribbling, or overwriting is strictly forbidden as they destroy the original record.

questions.q: Good Laboratory Practice requires all physical observations to be recorded objectively, utilizing unambiguous, quantitative language whenever possible. Which of the following lab notebook entries best meets the standard for an objective observation record?
options: The bacterial pellet appeared normal in size and was a good shade of white.
Following centrifugation at $4000 \times g$ for 10 minutes, an off-white pellet measuring approximately $2 \text{ mm}$ in diameter was visible at the bottom of the tube.
The centrifugation step yielded a lot of precipitate, proving that the cellular lysis step worked perfectly.
A huge, healthy-looking cellular pellet was successfully formed after spinning the sample.
questions.explain:
Objective documentation must avoid subjective interpretations (like "normal," "good," "huge," "a lot," or "healthy-looking"). 

Option 'b' is the only choice that provides factual, measurable data: it states the conditions ($4000 \times g$ for 10 minutes), color ("off-white"), and a quantitative estimate of size ("approximately $2 \text{ mm}$"), leaving no room for subjective misinterpretation by future readers.

questions.q: To prevent biological contamination during a sensitive mammalian cell culture procedure, a technician writes their volume calculations and timepoints on the paper sleeve of a sterile pipette, intending to transfer the data into the official laboratory notebook at the end of the week. Which core principle of data integrity does this practice most directly violate?
questions.explain:
This practice violates the principle that data must be **Contemporaneous** (the 'C' in ALCOA). 

Contemporaneous means data must be recorded in the official designated system *at the exact time* the work is performed. Writing notes on scraps of paper, gloves, or pipette sleeves to transcribe days later creates massive risks for memory errors, transcription errors, or lost data. While it also touches on 'Original' (since the pipette sleeve becomes the uncontrolled original record), the delayed transcription is a primary violation of contemporaneous recording.
